name: Drip
summary: Ecommerce email and onsite marketing built around your store's order data — segments, abandoned-cart and welcome playbooks, pop-ups and A/B testing, with one-click links to Shopify, WooCommerce and BigCommerce.
best_for: an online store on Shopify, WooCommerce or BigCommerce that already has order data worth segmenting and wants ecommerce playbooks — abandoned cart, welcome series, post-purchase — without assembling them by hand. The pricing model suits a list that grows steadily and mails at a normal cadence, because you pay for people rather than per seat or per feature, and every plan carries the whole feature set
skip_if: you are not selling online: Drip says an ecommerce store is not required but that the platform is built for one, and you would be paying for the half you cannot use. Skip it too if your list is large and you mail often, because the send allowance caps at twelve per contact per month once you are past the small tiers. The same goes past 175,000 people, where the published ladder ends and pricing becomes a conversation
honest_knock: The word “unlimited” quietly expires. At the prices most small shops pay, the send allowance really is uncapped. But the switch has an exact address: unlimited holds to 30,000 people, and from 30,001 the bullet becomes a hard number — 390,000 sends there, 600,000 at 50,000 people, twelve per contact per month. Drip never flags the switch. If you run a daily-deal or high-frequency list, do the arithmetic before you migrate: twelve sends per contact is generous for a monthly newsletter and tight for anything that mails several times a week. The second thing to price in is service. The card looks the same at every level, but two lines on it are not: you cannot talk to anyone in chat until $99/month, and free migration and personalized onboarding only appear from 15,001 people ($249). Below those thresholds it is email support and your own move, which is a real difference on the day a broken automation is sending to the wrong segment.

pricing.notes: (ladder re-read on drip.com/pricing on 17 September 2026; every rung below was confirmed on the live slider and matches the page's own pricing object) One ladder, no tiers: you drag a slider to your list size and Drip prints a monthly price. The page now headlines it as paying for your list size and how many emails you send. 1-2,500 people is $39, then $49 at 3,000, $59 at 3,500, $69 at 4,000, $79 at 4,500, $89 at 5,000, $99 at 6,000, $109 at 7,000, $124 at 8,000, $139 at 9,000, $154 at 10,000, $169 at 12,500, $209 at 15,000, $249 at 17,500, $289 at 20,000, $329 at 22,500, $369 at 25,000, $409 at 27,500, $449 at 30,000 and $489 at 32,500; from there it climbs $40 a rung to $609 at 40,000, $649 at 45,000 and $699 at 50,000, after which every extra 5,000 people costs $50 — $1,299 at 110,000, $1,949 at 175,000, and a last published rung of $1,999 for 175,001-180,000 people. Above 180,000 the price is replaced by “Let’s chat”, though the card keeps printing a send allowance. The trial is 14 days and takes no card, and their FAQ states unlimited emails are not available during it. Three things the ladder does not advertise. Chat support is not included at the entry price: up to 5,000 people the line reads “Email support”, and “Chat and email support” only appears from $99 (6,000 people). “Unlimited email sends” stops being literally true at 30,001 people, where the bullet becomes “390,000 email sends” and every rung above it carries exactly twelve sends a month per person at the top of the bracket — 600,000 at 50,000 people, 2,160,000 at 180,000. And the card is not the same at every rung: free migration and personalized onboarding appear from 15,001 people ($249) and are absent on every rung below that. What is carried at every price is up to 50 workflows, unlimited sub-accounts, open API access, dynamic segments, onsite campaigns and the Drip MCP connection, which their FAQ describes as included at no extra cost.

compare_with.name: Klaviyo
compare_with.why: the comparison Drip picks itself — it publishes a Drip vs. Klaviyo page — and the one most ecommerce teams actually make. Both price on list size and both live off store data; the practical question is what the send allowance and the support line look like at your volume, which is where Drip's ladder is unusually easy to read and unusually quiet about the twelve-sends ceiling
